newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Hashimoto hold friendly, informal chat.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Hashimoto hold friendly, informal chat.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto chatted informally over coffee late on Thursday night in a warm start to a two-day visit to Washington by the Japanese leader.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton and Hashimoto were "teasing each other and bantering around a little bit" in the Oval Office before Clinton went to the press briefing room to deliver remarks praising the Senate's passage of a chemical weapons treaty.

After Clinton's remarks, which Hashimoto watched on television in the Oval Office, Clinton rejoined his guest. They went over to the White House residence for what McCurry described as "a social visit that would no doubt border on the substantive."
The two leaders are to hold official talks on Friday.
A key topic that Hashimoto had on his mind was whether Clinton would be raising specific trade issues during their talks.
Japan's trade surplus with the United States rose 11.2 percent to $3.04 billion in March, the sixth consecutive month in which it had risen year-on-year.

"The first thing I want to find out when I arrive in Washington is whether President (Bill) Clinton will bring up specific trade issues," Hashimoto told reporters travelling with him from Tokyo to Washington.

Dissatisfied with slow growth in sales of American goods and services in Japan, Washington has been calling for progress in bilateral negotiations over such issues as automobiles, airline service, shipyards and telecommunications.
Japan wants the summit to be a venue for an exchange of opinions on world affairs such as the situation in the Korean peninsula and aid to poverty-stricken African nations.
The White House has made clear those topics will be discussed and that trade will not be a dominant issue.
But the Washington Post said Clinton had sent a blunt letter to Hashimoto earlier this month warning that Tokyo's economic policies raise the risk of a dangerous surge in Japan's trade surplus.

"I am concerned ... about a resumed cycle of large Japanese trade imbalances, financial market tension and protectionist pressures," Clinton wrote in the letter, delivered by Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin on a trip to Tokyo.

The president admonished that Japan's efforts to curb its budget deficit "may undermine" Japan's economic recovery and "lead to a significant increase" in the trade surplus which totalled $62 billion last year.

A White House official, while not giving out a copy of the letter, said that it "encourages Prime Minister Hashimoto to ensure that any changes in his fiscal policy take account of the need to maintain growth and doemstic demand in the Japanese economy."
The White House said Clinton's Thursday night meeting with Hashimoto was in keeping with the president's informal style. McCurry described Hashimoto as a "close friend" of Clinton.
"They want to meet outside the strict, formal setting of a summit meeting," said White House spokeswoman Mary Ellen Glynn. "That's President Clinton's style. It's the way he likes to do business."
Earlier this month, Clinton had invited visiting Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien to the White House for a chat on the night before their formal talks.
